articles.description:
Mississippi has elected the Democrat Scott Colom in a historic race in the traditionally deep-red state, making him its first Black senator since shortly after the US civil war. The closely contested race was called more than a week after the US midterms, with Colom running against the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. How did Colom’s grassroots campaign win despite limited early backing from national Democrats? Lucy Hough speaks to politics and democracy reporter George Chidi
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mississippi makes history with Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win - The Latest

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright , produced by Anabel Bacon and Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Jonathan Menjivar
articles.description:
Pete Hegseth has managed to dodge an impeachment trial, for the second time. And Republicans have avoided — for now — a major public accounting of the damage done at the Pentagon during Hegseth’s tenure. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment detail charges that are likely to return when Democrats take the majority next year. Kai Wright speaks with Guardian senior political enterprise reporter Aram Roston about how people inside the military have reacted to the impeachment and to Hegseth’s tenure, from the boat strikes in the Caribbean to the massive loss of experienced leadership and a dramatic depletion of munitions in Iran. Roston, who has covered the Pentagon across several administrations, describes a Pentagon shaken up in ways he’s never before seen.

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pete Hegseth’s wake of destruction at the Pentagon – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Phillip Inman
articles.description:
Wage growth falls to to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people

Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release a major report on the youth jobs crisis.
The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had expected it to remain at 4.7%.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6%, as government prepares to release Milburn report

articles.author: Anna Tims
articles.description:
A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796
My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86.
I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote

articles.author: Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores
Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.
But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1m), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market

articles.author: Matthew Pearce
articles.description:
About a third of cases involved chemicals banned for use on EU farms, according to investigation by Unearthed and Public Eye 
Pesticides sold by European chemical companies were named in more than 1,600 poisoning reports in Brazil last year, an investigation has found.
About a third of the cases involved chemicals banned from use on farms in the EU because of the risks they pose to people and the environment. But European companies are not banned from manufacturing these chemicals, as long as they export them overseas to countries where they are legally allowed to be used.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: European-made pesticides named in 1,605 poisoning reports in Brazil last year

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign is very selective with its figures
A new analysis from some of the architects of the Vote Leave campaign has claimed rejoining the EU would cost Britain £750m a week. How did they arrive at these figures – and are they any more reliable than the ones on the side of the bus?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is £750m a week the real cost of rejoining the EU – or the Brexit bus myth all over again?

articles.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
articles.description:
Campaigners call for reopening of high-speed Eurostar stations and new infrastructure for London St Pancras
Britain should throw its weight behind international rail services to reset the UK-EU relationship, transport campaigners have urged the prime minister.
A coalition of groups has called on Andy Burnham to commit to reopening high-speed stations for Eurostar and other services in Kent, and to support new infrastructure for passengers at London St Pancras and for rail freight.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Invest in international rail services to boost UK-EU reset, Burnham urged

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Many of those onboard are being deported for second time after fleeing threats from people smugglers in France
Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation flight are people who returned to the UK fleeing threats from smugglers after they were already forcibly returned to France.
Hundreds of asylum seekers who were sent back to France are thought to have returned to the UK, citing threats from smugglers who said their families still owed them money for the Channel crossing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Asylum seekers on final ‘one in, one out’ UK-France flight feel they are being ‘punished’

articles.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
articles.description:
Bringing the number not in education, employment or training down from a decade high will be tough. Here’s why

Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

Almost a million young people – one in eight – in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Having reached the highest level in a decade, the government is seeking to bring that number down after the recommendations made in Alan Milburn’s landmark report.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts

articles.author: Pippa Crerar and Lisa O’Carroll
articles.description:
Prime minister signals Labour could drop its Brexit red lines in major foreign policy speech
Britain’s global standing has diminished in the decade since Brexit, Andy Burnham has said, as he again signalled that Labour could drop its red lines on Europe in its next manifesto.
In a foreign policy speech, Burnham said that after a major Brussels summit this week he would begin new discussions with the EU about options for “our long-term relationship”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Burnham says Brexit has dramatically diminished Britain’s global standing

articles.author: Richard Partington, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu
articles.description:
Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up
Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits.
In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Home Office plans will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety, say refugee charities
Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow immigration enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Refused UK asylum seekers to lose five-day grace period and face immediate removal

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it
Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

articles.author: Pippa Crerar Political editor
articles.description:
Labour grandee seems to have assuaged MPs’ nerves on need for welfare reform to tackle youth unemployment crisis
In a boxing gym in Peterborough almost a year ago, Alan Milburn, freshly appointed to run a government review into the nearly 1 million young people out of work and education, said he would be “unafraid to shine a light on uncomfortable truths”.
The Labour grandee, who held three cabinet jobs under Tony Blair, warned there was a “downward escalator” taking young people into a “world of benefits” and vowed to provide radical solutions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Milburn won over Labour on tackling rising youth unemployment

articles.author: Mark Sweney
articles.description:
Big-screen debut of Ian Fleming’s creation in 1962, with Sean Connery as lead in Dr No, was start of marketing dream

New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson

Share your thoughts on the casting

Peter Bradshaw’s take

Robert Pattinson’s journey to James Bond

James Bond may be 73 years old but the superspy holds a licence to print money, at the centre of an evergreen multibillion-pound franchise spanning blockbuster films, merchandise, licensing deals and sponsorship.
The announcement that the Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson is the next Bond comes seven years after Daniel Craig revealed that No Time To Die would be his last outing as 007.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The man with the golden touch: James Bond franchise is a money-spinner

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Comments come after Mia Latter, who alleged she was raped by Russell Brand, had said she wanted a change in law
A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggered age of consent.
Walliams, 55, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found.
Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse, childhood abuse, and people in crisis.
The ITV News documentary David Walliams: Power and Silence is available to watch on YouTube and ITVX.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Woman accusing David Walliams of grooming her backs staggered age of consent call

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.description:
Brand’s wife Laura read out a message from him on their YouTube show
After education questions, there is one urgent question in the Commons and two ministerial statements. They are, with rough timings:
3.30pm: A Home Office minister responds to an urgent question about planning permission being granted for the proposed camp for asylum seekers near Piddington.
It’s always a good idea to promote closer cooperation with all of our allies, and there’s always more that you can do to facilitate trade with friends and neighbours. However, what I disagree with is a settlement that will involve us paying hundreds of millions of pounds into the EU and involve the imposition of huge amounts of red tape on all sorts of businesses across the country … I think it’s a really bad step backwards.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brand statement from prison claiming his innocence ‘appalling’ and could breach rules, says No 10 – as it happened

articles.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
articles.description:
Forces across England and Wales struggle amid financial pressures described as worst for decades
Police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government.
Paul Sanford, the chief constable of Norfolk police and the finance lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), said exceptional financial support was needed if forces across England and Wales were to remain operationally viable.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police ‘retreating from streets’ due to major funding crisis, chief constables say

articles.author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
articles.description:
Renowned centre of Shakespeare studies, which is part of University of Birmingham, to move to its Edgbaston campus 
“Near-philistine”, “ignorant”, “unbelievably stupid”, “terrible”, “extraordinarily sad and shortsighted”, “an appalling act of cultural vandalism”, “a disaster” and “an absolute disgrace”.
Such has been the furious reaction to news that the Shakespeare Institute, a much-loved and internationally renowned centre of scholarship, is to leave its home in Stratford-upon-Avon, the playwright’s place of birth, and move to Birmingham.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Near-philistine’: fury greets Shakespeare Institute plan to leave Stratford-upon-Avon

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Presenter says she will remain at the corporation working on show launching in 2027, as search for successor begins
The BBC has confirmed Emma Barnett is stepping down as a presenter of Radio 4’s Today programme, setting off the broadcaster’s latest search for a new name to co-host its flagship news programme.
The official announcement came after months of speculation about Barnett’s future on the show. Her last appearance will be broadcast on Wednesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Emma Barnett steps down from BBC Radio 4’s Today programme

articles.author: Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
Brand reacted with ‘shock and dismay’ after products were also found in a ‘bargain bin inside a gas station’
David Beckham’s company reacted with “shock and dismay” after discovering his branded fragrance range was on sale in petrol stations and in the British discount store Poundland, court documents have revealed.
The former England football captain’s brand, DB Ventures, has launched a lawsuit against the distributor of the products, arguing it allowed them to be sold in stores that had not been agreed upon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Beckham firm sues after fragrance found for sale in discount store

articles.author: Presented by Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Annie La Vespa, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
It is a big week for Andy Burnham as two of his big policy priorities enter the spotlight. On Tuesday, the Milburn review of welfare for under-25s is published, which could ignite old Labour tensions over benefit cuts.
Then, later this week, Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit to discuss a potential new deal. But, as Pippa has signalled, cabinet ministers have told Burnham to put the brake on some of the discussions to ensure the government is not out of step with the public.
Is it too little too late?
You can read Rowena Mason’s article on benefits for under-25s here.
You can watch episodes of Politics Weekly on our YouTube channel here.
Send your questions to Pippa and Kiran on politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will Burnham put a ‘brake’ on push to rejoin EU – podcast

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Popular edible golden oyster classed as high-risk invasive species because of negative impact on woodlands
They have been viewed for years as the ideal Christmas gift for the culinary-minded, but experts have now warned that grow-your-own mushroom kits should be blacklisted from a spot under the tree.
An international group of mycologists, including experts from the Royal Horticultural Society, have said many of these kits, which allow people to easily grow mushrooms at home as a delicious addition to stir-fries and other dishes, contain invasive species.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Move reflects growing demand for outdoor swimming as Britain heats up and follows campaign by MPs
Andy Burnham is setting up a public fund to rebuild the UK’s lidos after a revival in outdoor swimming.
Outdoor pools were built across the UK in the 1930s. The often beautiful, art deco constructions were made as a cheap way to provide access to healthy activity during the summer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Under-threat lidos get lifeline as Andy Burnham sets up fund to rebuild pools

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds

Business live – latest updates

Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in a near £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.
The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for soaring subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Move follows Russell Brand trial, in which his barrister argued comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not ‘resisted’

UK politics live – latest updates

Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial.
Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers amid concern over the tactics deployed by the comedian’s counsel. In his letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Norris said it was “unacceptable” for the profession to “perpetuate myths” about rape victims in court, and warned that those who broke the rules could face disciplinary action.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Barristers could be barred from practice over use of rape myths, warns justice secretary

articles.author: Denis Campbell Health policy editor
articles.description:
Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say
UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter.
Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches

articles.author: Denis Campbell and Hanad Ahmed
articles.description:
NHS chiefs said last year that 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England do not meet safety standards
Ministers have been accused of “gambling with the safety of mothers and babies” after admitting they do not know how much repairing decrepit maternity units would cost.
NHS chiefs said last year that shoddy infrastructure meant 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England did not meet basic safety standards. Infrastructure problems hampered the delivery of clinical care thousands of times every year, NHS England said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ministers accused of ‘gambling with safety’ for not knowing cost of NHS maternity unit repairs

articles.author: Lyndsey Winship
articles.description:
Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing
Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.
“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart

articles.author: Harry Taylor
articles.description:
UKHSA warns of health impact on those vulnerable to cold and urges people to check in with neighbours 
Cold weather warnings have been issued for parts of the UK, and alerts for the risk to health services are due to begin on Sunday evening.
The Met Office issued yellow weather warnings for ice for central and eastern Scotland from 6pm on Sunday evening until 10am on Monday. People should be vigilant as they travelled, due to the risk from slipping on footpaths in icy conditions, it added.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cold and health alerts issued for Scotland and northern England as snow and ice expected

articles.author: Anna Bawden
articles.description:
Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership
Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.
The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS England on track to miss key cancer treatment target by 10,000 patients

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Activists dumped rocks off Norfolk coast on site of Burnham-backed project in protest against seabed trawling
The giant offshore windfarms backed by Andy Burnham this week may face unexpected stumbling blocks after Greenpeace activists unwittingly dumped about 15 tonnes of boulders on to the site as part of a campaign against seabed trawling in the North Sea.
Greenpeace created the “boulder barrier” to safeguard harbour porpoises off the Norfolk coast by dropping giant stone blocks, each weighing up to 2 tonnes, on to the sea floor to prevent a method of fishing known as bottom trawling.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Greenpeace boulders may delay building of £12bn windfarms in North Sea

articles.author: Joe Pinner
articles.description:
Five-year project will create wildlife corridors by building wetlands and increase access to green and blue spaces
Bristol could become home to the UK’s first “wetland city” thanks to a charity’s efforts to create vast wildlife corridors that will reduce flood risk and give people more access to green and blue spaces.
The Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (WWT) said the five-year initiative would include more than 200 projects to restore and create wetlands across the city. These will range from small household rainwater ponds and street-level rain gardens to restoring river habitats, reconnecting rivers with their floodplains, and creating new wetlands.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bristol aims to become UK’s first ‘wetland city’ and reduce flood risk

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back
The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?
Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank

articles.author: Vikram Dodd and Hannah Al-Othman
articles.description:
Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents have had to find a workaround for Microsoft packages
Hospitals, GPs, police forces and property agents across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage. Here’s how the disruption to email and other IT facilities has affected key services.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Microsoft outage has affected key public services in the UK

articles.author: Daniel Boffey Chief reporter
articles.description:
It has been suggested that women with stories to tell felt silenced after signing non-disclosure agreements
The UK’s minister for women has suggested that the government has not gone far enough in tackling the abusive use of non-disclosure agreements.
Bridget Phillipson was commenting in the context of the allegations of improper behaviour by David Walliams – which he denies – and the conviction of Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault. In both cases, it has been suggested that women with stories to tell felt silenced after signing an NDA.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: After Walliams and Brand, how could the UK government tackle NDAs?

articles.description:
Multiple women allege David Walliams abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were young women, an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. He denies the allegations. Maeve McClenaghan reports
David Walliams, the comedian and former Britain’s Got Talent judge, is alleged to have groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

articles.description:
Multiple women allege David Walliams abused his power and position as a celebrity to prey on them for sexual purposes when they were young women, an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found. He denies the allegations.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on this investigation, Walliams writes: 'Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

'I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.'

He adds: 'I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.'

Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault

articles.author: Josh Halliday North of England editor
articles.description:
Residents of Astley in Greater Manchester will tell public inquiry next week of ‘cacophony’ of noise causing sleep deprivation and depression
When Stephen Retford retired from the police in 2006, he looked forward to a quiet life after nearly three decades catching villains. But now the former detective has landed another big case – one that is extremely close to home.
“It’s the total injustice of it,” the 70-year-old seethed, staring up at the 18-metre-high mega-warehouse that looms over the quiet village of Astley in Greater Manchester. Residents are up in arms about the “monster” construction, likening it to having a “cruise ship in our back garden”.

articles.title: ‘It’s a feeling of being screwed over’: once-quiet village despairs over ‘monster’ warehouse

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
Scheme in Derry aims to sow confidence by getting people with learning and physical disabilities into wrestling
The music thumped, the lights blazed and from the ring the announcer did a countdown. “Who is ready to rumble?” he roared. The bellows and cheers indicated that the crowd at St Columb’s Hall in Derry on Saturday night was more than ready for the Foyle Rumble, and so began a wrestling extravaganza of heroes and villains in leotards, masks and kneepads.
The blend of athleticism and scripted storytelling would have been familiar to fans of WrestleMania, but this Northern Irish version came with a twist: many of the performers have learning or physical disabilities, and the characters they play in the ring do not quite stay in the ring.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘No matter what, he doesn’t quit’: disabled wrestlers draw strength from ring alter egos

articles.author: Chris Osuh, Aamna Mohdin and Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Some relatives of British citizens say they feel left behind, but announcement has brought relief to many care workers
“The only time we’re regarded as human beings is when they need a lot of hands onboard, like during Covid. But after that, we’re tossed away like we’re some rubbish,” Aneisha Williams says.
Williams, 39, was months from qualifying for indefinite leave to remain after 10 years in the UK. But claiming housing benefit could delay her settlement for years under Shabana Mahmood’s “earned settlement” plans.

articles.title: ‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions

Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
With heir apparent Danny Tommo also in custody, Robinson’s conviction for harassing journalists is blow to anti-migrant movement
The verdict was met with a groan from Tommy Robinson’s supporters, who had sat behind the dock throughout his harassment trial.
It took more than 11 hours of jury deliberations to find the far-right activist guilty of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists, enough time for a band of lieutenants and hangers-on to get their hopes up that he might be acquitted.

articles.author: Tom McIlroy in Manila
articles.description:
Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China’s efforts to dominate

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the two leaders meet on Tuesday, as Australia signed on to a US-led pact to secure the technologies ​and critical infrastructure for artificial intelligence supply chains.
The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Lauren Almeida
articles.description:
As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’
Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.
The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO

articles.author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya
articles.description:
While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged

Cop31 live – latest updates

Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.
While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports

articles.author: Lewis Gordon
articles.description:
Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact
• The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
• Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus
• Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA
A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline.
The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world

CEO ousted after affair with suspected Chinese spy reportedly plans comeback, but US treasury secretary urges ‘dramatic shake-up’

An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

articles.description:
Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design
Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.
It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis
Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found.
While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.

articles.title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’

articles.author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
articles.description:
Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s software
The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it.
As Guardian Australia reported in September, Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare.

articles.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software

articles.author: Jackson Ryan
articles.description:
Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind
A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days.
The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype
It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.
The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI

articles.author: Agencies

Fears for national college entrance exam next week as test taker admits sending photos of questions to AI tool
The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true. On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.
The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

articles.title: 160 questions, only one wrong: top scorer in South Korea tax exam admits AI cheating

Unlike familiar Captcha tests, this con asks you to press a series of keys. And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software
You are looking for some gifts for Christmas and want to support small businesses when you shop. When you visit the site of one you’ve heard good things about you are asked to verify that you are human.

Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true
The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech giant and Meta says it plans to appeal the decision
Italy’s data protection agency has fined Facebook parent company Meta €805m ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their specific consent.
Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement.

Tech company says operations restored to all customers and regions affected by one of worst IT failures in years
Microsoft has said its service has been fully restored after a massive outage that resulted in widespread disruption to governments, businesses and public services around the world.

Once the ultimate symbol of Hollywood rebellion, the former Nvidia chief’s signature look is now being mocked as a midlife crisis cliche
For nearly two decades a black leather jacket has been a key part of Jensen Huang’s look. Now it has become a punchline.

articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
articles.description:
Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House
In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.
After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda

articles.description:
Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited
This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration
Arriving alongside November’s blue wave, Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together.
It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country, except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it.
